To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the ability to learn a concept from negative examples alone is not sufficient to learn a concept in the limit from a teacher that can give only negative examples; and (2) the ability to "correct" positive examples gives more power to a one-shot learner than the ability to receive only negative (counter) examples.

(1) one-shot learner with access to positive examples and negative counterexamples is more powerful than the one-shot learner with only negative counterexamples and (2) the former learner is as powerful as the one-shot learner that has access to full positive and negative data

(i) the ability to "correct" positive examples is sometimes more powerful than just receiving negative examples, (ii) in some cases, the ability to "rephrase" positive examples is more powerful than just negative examples and full access to positive data, and (iii) the ability to rephrase positive examples can sometimes give a learner the power to learn from one-shot examples.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is a role of overt and covert negative evidence in the process of language acquisition? How much information is necessary for a learner in order to learn a language?
a formal study of the role of negative examples and positive examples in language acquisition.
the following questions: How can a learner make use of negative evidence and corrected positive examples to learn a language? What is the complexity of such learning?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, the best approach is a combination of negative counterexamples and nearest positive examples, which is also the most natural approach.
one-shot learners" are not necessarily weaker than "full-data learners", and that the former can be even better in terms of query complexity.
, depending on a type of a model of learning, one type of evidence is sometimes more advantageous over another, sometimes not, and sometimes both types of evidence are equally powerful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more evidence we get from a teacher, the better we can learn, where the best is to get all positive and all negative examples.
, in some cases, one-shot learners can be very efficient and can achieve a high level of performance.
the more evidence a learner has, the more it knows, but the less it can learn.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in some cases, the learning power of a learner can be improved by providing a learner with a "corrected" positive example, instead of a counterexample, and that in some cases the learning power can be improved by access to a "nearby" positive example, rather than access to full positive examples.
in the process of language acquisition a child may be able to learn a language with a single negative counterexample and a nearest positive example.
, even if a learner has access to full positive examples, it may be better to ask for negative examples and corrected positive examples.
